## Introduction to the ADA Accommodation Requirement

The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) is a landmark civil rights law that prohibits discrimination against individuals with disabilities in all areas of public life, including employment, transportation, public accommodations, communications, and state and local government activities.[^1] A critical component of the ADA is the requirement that covered entities provide "reasonable accommodations" to qualified individuals with disabilities, unless doing so would impose an "undue hardship."[^2] This legal reference document will provide a comprehensive overview of the ADA's accommodation mandate, including the governing legal standards, the interactive process, and available remedies for non-compliance.

## Defining a "Reasonable Accommodation"

Under the ADA, a "reasonable accommodation" is a modification or adjustment to the work environment, or to the manner or circumstances under which a position is customarily performed, that enables a qualified individual with a disability to perform the essential functions of that position.[^3] The accommodation must be effective in enabling the individual to perform their job duties.[^4] Reasonable accommodations can include, but are not limited to, job restructuring, part-time or modified work schedules, acquisition or modification of equipment, the provision of qualified readers or interpreters, and other similar accommodations.[^5] Importantly, the ADA does not require employers to provide the "best" accommodation, only a reasonable one.[^6]

## The Interactive Process

Providing a reasonable accommodation is an interactive process between the employer and the qualified individual with a disability.[^7] The process begins when the individual requests an accommodation or the employer becomes aware of the need for one.[^8] The employer must then engage in an interactive dialogue with the individual to identify the precise limitations resulting from the disability and potential reasonable accommodations that could overcome those limitations.[^9] This interactive process is a mandatory obligation under the ADA, and failure to engage in it can constitute unlawful discrimination.[^10] 

The employer is entitled to request medical documentation to substantiate the existence of the disability and the need for accommodation, as long as the request is job-related and consistent with business necessity.[^11] Once the interactive process is initiated, the employer must work collaboratively with the individual to identify an effective accommodation, considering the preferences of the individual.[^12] If multiple effective accommodations are available, the employer has the discretion to choose which one to provide.[^13]

## The Undue Hardship Defense

Employers are not required to provide a reasonable accommodation if doing so would impose an "undue hardship" on the operation of the employer's business.[^14] Undue hardship is defined as an action requiring significant difficulty or expense, when considered in light of factors such as the nature and cost of the accommodation, the overall financial resources of the facility, the number of employees, and the impact of the accommodation on the operation of the facility.[^15] The employer bears the burden of proving that a proposed accommodation would cause an undue hardship.[^16]

Courts have found undue hardship in a variety of circumstances, such as where the accommodation would require the employer to fundamentally alter the nature of its business,[^17] create a direct threat to the health or safety of the individual or others,[^18] or result in significant disruption to the workflow and productivity of the workplace.[^19] However, the undue hardship analysis is highly fact-specific, and employers cannot rely on mere speculation or assumptions about hardship.[^20]

## Enforcement and Remedies

Individuals who are denied a reasonable accommodation in violation of the ADA may file a charge of discrimination with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC).[^21] If the EEOC finds reasonable cause to believe that discrimination has occurred, it will attempt to resolve the matter through conciliation.[^22] If conciliation fails, the EEOC may file a lawsuit against the employer on behalf of the individual.[^23]

Alternatively, the individual may bypass the EEOC process and file a private lawsuit directly against the employer in federal court.[^24] Successful plaintiffs in ADA accommodation cases may be entitled to remedies such as back pay, front pay, reinstatement, compensatory damages for emotional distress, and attorneys' fees and costs.[^25] In egregious cases involving intentional discrimination, punitive damages may also be available.[^26]

## Conclusion

The ADA's reasonable accommodation requirement is a critical protection for individuals with disabilities in the workplace. Employers must engage in a good-faith interactive process to identify and provide effective accommodations, unless doing so would pose an undue hardship. Failure to comply with this mandate can result in significant legal liability for employers. By understanding and adhering to the ADA's accommodation standards, employers can foster an inclusive and accessible work environment for all qualified individuals.
